text: To lavish something on a person or a thing is to give it generously, in large amounts, often more than seems necessary. The headline says China lavishes attention on this competition: state television every day, huge ceremonies, hundreds of training centres. The word quietly asks whether all that attention is deserved.

Crushed usually means squashed flat, but in sport and contests it means beaten very badly. Team China crushed its rivals here: 41 golds against about four for South Korea, the next best country. Nothing was physically squashed.

Your rivals are the people or teams you compete against for the same prize. The word suggests a contest that keeps going rather than one match — the two best schools in a league are rivals year after year. China's rivals here are the other 60-odd countries that sent competitors.

WorldSkills is an international contest, held every two years, where young people compete at practical trades: bricklaying, welding, gardening, machine work, train repair. Spain started it in 1950 to push more teenagers into apprenticeships. People sometimes call it the skills Olympics, and this year's was held in Shanghai.
The runner-up is whoever finishes second. South Korea was the runner-up at this competition, with about a tenth of China's golds. The plural is runners-up.

An extravaganza is a huge, showy, expensive event — more spectacle than the occasion really needs. Calling the six days in Shanghai an extravaganza tells you about the lights, ceremonies and dancing robots, not about the welding. It comes from the same root as extravagant.
To wrap something up is to finish it off. A meeting, a tournament or a school year can all wrap up. The competition wrapped up in Shanghai on September 27th, meaning that was its last day.

Sticking -odd onto a number means roughly that many, a little more or a little less: 60-odd countries is about 60. Writers use it when the exact count does not matter. It has nothing to do with being strange.

A panel is normally a flat piece of wood or glass, but it also means a small group of people chosen to judge or discuss something. Competitors here worked in front of panels of judges. You meet the same use in a panel of experts or a quiz-show panel.

Amid means in the middle of, or surrounded by. It is the formal cousin of among, and what it surrounds you with is usually noise, danger or activity rather than objects. The competitors worked amid Olympic-style razzmatazz.

Razzmatazz is noisy, flashy showing-off meant to excite a crowd: lights, music, announcers, fireworks. It is a playful and slightly mocking word. Here it describes the Olympic-style spectacle China wrapped around a bricklaying contest.

A jamboree is a big, cheerful gathering or celebration — the word is used for scout rallies and music festivals. Saying this was no sporting jamboree makes the point that the event was serious work, not a party.

Bricklaying is the trade of building walls out of bricks, setting each one in wet mortar so the rows stay level and the corners stay square. It is skilled work: speed, straightness and clean joints are all judged. At WorldSkills it is a medal event.

Machining is shaping metal by cutting it, using machine tools such as lathes and mills that shave material away until the part matches a drawing exactly. Almost every engine and machine contains machined parts. The allowed error is a fraction of a millimetre, which is what makes it a competition skill.

Landscape gardening is designing and building outdoor spaces: laying paths and low walls, shaping the ground, planting so the result looks right and survives. It is part garden design and part construction. France beat China in this event.

Resources are whatever you have available to spend on something: money, equipment, buildings, people's time. China has poured more resources into this contest than any other country — bases, coaches, airtime. In other contexts the word means natural resources, like oil or timber.

An arena is the floor of a stadium where a contest happens, but writers also use it for the contest itself, or for any place where people compete. Saying China sees benefits far beyond the arena means the gains come outside the competition — in pride and in diplomacy. Nobody is talking about a building.

A headline is the large line of type at the top of a news story, so to make headlines is to get big news coverage. Something that rarely makes headlines is mostly ignored by the press. This tournament makes headlines in China and almost none in the West.

The West, with a capital W, is not a direction here. It is shorthand for the wealthy countries of western Europe and North America, plus places like Australia, grouped together by shared history and politics. The article says this competition rarely makes news there.

An apprenticeship is a way of learning a skilled trade by doing it: you work beside an expert for a few years, get paid while you learn, and come out qualified. Electricians, plumbers, chefs and mechanics are often trained this way. Spain launched this competition in 1950 to encourage more young people into apprenticeships.

Welding is joining two pieces of metal by melting their edges so the molten metal runs together and hardens into one piece. It takes a very hot flame or an electric arc, a steady hand and a dark mask. China's first ever medal at this contest was a silver in welding.

Routinely means regularly, as a matter of routine — the normal thing rather than a one-off. Saying China now routinely dominates the event means winning has become its usual result instead of a surprise.

To dominate something is to be so much stronger than everyone else that you control how it goes. In a contest it simply means winning most of what there is to win. China dominates WorldSkills: 41 golds, ten times as many as the runner-up.

Discipline often means rules and punishment, but it has a second, completely different meaning: a field of study or skill. Competitors complete tasks in their discipline — welding, gardening, train repair. School subjects are disciplines too, which is why a historian and a chemist work in different ones.

A wind turbine is a tall tower with long blades that spin in the wind and turn a generator, which makes electricity. One task at the competition was installing, testing and repairing a wind-turbine component, meaning a single part of such a machine. Keeping thousands of turbines running is real and growing work.

A component is one part of a bigger machine or system, built to fit together with the rest. A bicycle's brake lever is a component, and so is the gearbox inside a wind turbine. Engineers like the word because it implies the part was designed to belong somewhere.

Precision is exactness: doing something so carefully that the result matches the measurement almost perfectly. Competitors earn points for speed and precision, and those two often pull against each other — hurry, and the cut goes crooked. The adjective is precise.

Something elaborate is built from many carefully arranged parts instead of being simple, and the word hints at effort and detail. China's training system is elaborate: contests at three levels to decide who gets in, then hundreds of special bases with expert coaches. Watch out for the verb elaborate, as in could you elaborate, which means to explain in more detail.

Promising here has nothing to do with making a promise. It describes someone who shows early signs of becoming very good: a promising young swimmer, a promising student. China picks out promising young people and feeds them into its contests.

A filter catches some things and lets others through, so to be filtered through a series of contests means being sorted stage by stage, with most people dropping out each time. Promising young Chinese are filtered through local, provincial and national rounds before they reach the training system. Nothing is being strained through paper.

A province is a large region that a country is divided into, with its own government below the national one — China has about 30, Canada has ten. Provincial means belonging to that level, so a provincial contest sits between the local and the national one. The closest American equivalent is a state.

To designate something is to officially name it for a particular purpose. China has designated hundreds of bases for training competitors, which means the government picked them and gave them that job. You meet the word in designated driver and designated hitter.

A base is a place a group works out of and returns to, as in an army base. Here the bases are hundreds of training centres at colleges, universities and companies where competitors practise under coaches. It is not about baseball or the bottom of something.

Vocational schooling teaches you one specific skilled job instead of a general academic subject. Vocation is an old word for the work you do with your life, so a vocational college trains welders, nurses, electricians and cooks by having them do the work. Many Chinese look down on these colleges, which is exactly what their government is trying to change.

A drill is a tool that makes holes, but to drill a skill is to practise it over and over until it becomes automatic. Contestants drill their skills under specialist coaches, the way a team drills free throws. Soldiers drill too.

A specialist knows one narrow area extremely well, rather than a little about many things. A doctor who treats only eyes is a specialist. These competitors are coached by specialist coaches, sometimes past champions in the same trade.

Psychological means having to do with the mind: thoughts, feelings, nerves. Competitors get physical and psychological preparation, so somebody trains their bodies and somebody else helps them stay steady in front of judges and cameras. Psychology is the study of the mind.

An inspection is a careful official check to see whether something is safe or working properly. The gold medallist's event was train inspection, maintenance and repair: go over the train, find the faults, fix them. Restaurants and elevators get inspections too.

Maintenance is the routine work of keeping something running before it breaks: oiling, cleaning, tightening, swapping out worn parts. A train needs far more hours of maintenance than of repair. The verb is maintain.

When you attribute something to a cause, you say that is what made it happen, and the word almost always takes to after it. A coach attributed this gold medallist's success to countless nights alone at the training base, rather than to luck or natural talent. Writers in science and history use this verb constantly, because they have to say what caused what.

Countless means too many to count, a vague way of saying a very large number. Countless nights at the training base is not a figure anybody added up; it just means a great many. Innumerable means the same thing.

As a verb, resolve means to settle something or decide firmly. As a noun, which is how it is used here, resolve means determination: the refusal to give up. The organisation called China unique in the resolve and scale of its embrace of WorldSkills, meaning it wants this badly and is doing it in a big way.

Scale here is not a weighing machine or a row of musical notes. It means the size or extent of something: the scale of China's effort is hundreds of bases, thousands of trainees and nightly television. Anything done on a large scale is done big.

An embrace is a hug, but to embrace an idea or an activity is to take it up eagerly and completely. China's embrace of WorldSkills means it has thrown itself into the competition. Nobody is hugging anything.

Awe is the feeling of being amazed and a little overwhelmed by something huge or impressive. Awestruck means struck by that feeling. The competition's own organisers wrote a slightly awestruck report about how hard China goes at this.

A pay-off is what you get back for the effort or money you put in. China's pay-offs from this contest are national pride and influence abroad, not prize money. The verb phrase pay off means to produce that result: the training paid off.

In writing about countries, the state means the government of a country. So state-run media are the newspapers, television channels and websites that the government owns and directs: its officials decide which stories lead the news and which never get made at all. That is why this competition got daily national coverage, aimed at China's industrial strengths and winners wrapped in the flag.

To broadcast is to send a programme out over television, radio or the internet so everybody can receive it at once. The past tense is also broadcast. Chinese state television broadcast coverage of the competition every day it ran.

Industrial means to do with industry: making things in factories, at scale, using machines. China's industrial strengths are what its factories are especially good at producing, such as drones. Industry is the activity; industrial is the adjective for it.
To drape cloth is to hang it loosely over something so it falls in folds. Winners draped in China's flag had the flag hung around their shoulders. The curtains called drapes come from the same word.

Crimson is a deep, rich red, darker and stronger than scarlet. China's flag is crimson, which is what the Weibo commenter means by the dazzling red of China. Precise colour words like this are worth knowing because writers use them to set a mood.

Light is dazzling when it is so bright that it makes you squint or see spots. Used about anything else, it means stunningly impressive. The commenter calls the red of China dazzling, and means both at once.

Weibo is a huge Chinese social-media site where people post short public messages, a bit like X, formerly Twitter. Quoting a Weibo comment is how a reporter shows what ordinary people are saying online in China. Posts there are monitored and sometimes removed, so it is not a complete picture of what people think.

A project is usually a piece of work you take on, but as a verb, with the stress on the second syllable, project means to send something outward — a projector projects light onto a screen. China uses these competitions to project soft power: to push its influence outward so other countries feel it. Same spelling, two very different jobs.

Soft power is getting other countries to admire you and want to copy you, instead of pressuring them with armies or money. Films, universities, pop music, sports victories and training schools are all soft power. China projects it by winning medals on television and running skills workshops in poorer countries.

Luban is a legendary Chinese carpenter and inventor from about 2,500 years ago, remembered as the patron of builders and craftsmen. China names the vocational-training centres it sets up abroad Luban workshops, and this year's medals were shaped like Luban locks: interlocking wooden puzzles said to be his invention. The name advertises that Chinese skill is ancient.

Something mythical comes from myth: the old stories a culture tells about gods, heroes and the distant past. Calling Luban a mythical carpenter signals that the stories about him are more legend than record. The word can also mean simply imaginary, as in a mythical creature.

A carpenter builds and repairs things out of wood: roof frames, stairs, doors, furniture. It is one of the oldest skilled trades and still one of the most needed. Luban, the figure China named its workshops after, was said to be a carpenter.

An institution is an established organisation with a particular job in society: a school, a hospital, a court, a bank. The word points at the organisation as a lasting thing, not at its building or at whoever works there today. Calling the Luban workshops institutions says they are meant to stay.

Diplomatic means to do with diplomacy: the way governments deal with each other by talking, visiting and making deals rather than fighting. A diplomatic gift is one country being friendly to another on purpose. Said of a person, it means tactful.

A sweetener is literally something that makes food sweeter, but in deals and politics it means a little extra thrown in to make an offer more attractive. Saying the Luban workshops are not just a diplomatic sweetener means they do more than buy goodwill: they also spread Chinese technology. Nothing edible is involved.

Standards here are not levels of quality or rules of behaviour. They are agreed technical specifications that let equipment work together: which plug fits which socket, which voltage, which screw thread, which radio signal. Whoever's standards a country adopts ends up buying the matching equipment for decades, which is why China wants to export its own.
To export something is to send it out of your own country to another one, usually to sell it. Goods get exported, but so do ideas, standards and training. The opposite is import.

Supposedly flags a claim the writer will not promise is true: people say so, but who knows. The medals were shaped like puzzles supposedly created by Luban himself, which is a good story rather than a documented fact. Allegedly and reportedly do the same job.

A prime minister is the head of a country's government, the person who runs it day to day, in countries where that job is separate from a president or a monarch. Li Qiang is China's prime minister, and he opened this competition with a speech. China's most powerful leader is a different person, Xi Jinping, who heads the Communist Party.

The global south is shorthand for the poorer, less industrialised countries, most of them in Africa, Latin America and southern Asia. It groups countries by wealth and history rather than by a line on a map — Australia is in the southern hemisphere and is not part of it. The phrase has largely replaced the older term third world.

To look down on something is to treat it as beneath you and not worth respect. Many Chinese look down on vocational colleges, as though they were only for people who could not get into university. The opposite is to look up to.

Underfunded means given less money than it needs to do its job properly. An underfunded college cannot buy good equipment or pay good teachers. The prefix under- does the work, as in underpaid and understaffed.

The staff of a place are the people who work there, so how it is staffed is who it has working in it and how many. Badly staffed means too few of them, or ones who are not very good. A well-staffed hospital has enough nurses on every shift.

A shortfall is the gap between how much of something you have and how much you need, and it usually comes with a number attached: a 10m shortfall in skilled workers means China is 10m short of what its factories need. You meet the word constantly with budgets and with water. It comes from the phrase to fall short.

In The Economist, an m after a number means million and a bn means billion, so 10m is 10,000,000. The shorthand saves space in a magazine that prints a lot of figures. A shortfall of 10m workers is larger than the whole population of many countries.
